fixes.explanation: Cousins it is. Abigail, Amasa's mother, and Zeruiah, Joab's mother, are sisters, so their sons are cousins. Joab is one of David's commanders, and he's the man Absalom replaced with Amasa. Cousins, and now they're on opposite sides of this fight.

The mothers settle this one. Amasa's mother is Abigail, and Joab's mother is Zeruiah (2 Samuel 17:25). Those are two different women, so these two aren't brothers. Abigail and Zeruiah are the sisters, which makes their sons cousins. Joab's actual brother is Abishai, who shows up in the next chapter as Zeruiah's son.
The text ties these two together by family. Abigail, Amasa's mother, is the sister of Zeruiah, Joab's mother. Their mothers are sisters, and that makes Amasa and Joab cousins.

The text doesn't say David sent word. The three men come to meet him, and they give their own reason: “The people have become hungry, exhausted, and thirsty in the wilderness.” I think that makes it feel like a gift.

Talking to Absalom first isn't in the plan. David's words about his son come a few verses later, when he commands the commanders to treat Absalom gently. Here he tells his troops, “I will surely march out with you as well.” So the king says he'll go out with them, at least for now.
True. David answers, “I will do whatever seems best to you…” Then he stands beside the gate while the troops march out by hundreds and by thousands. So he stays back, just as his people pleaded.
Fairly sounds reasonable, but it isn't the word David uses. He commands, “Treat the young man Absalom gently for my sake.” And he says it's for his sake.

The forest of Ephraim, friend. That's where David's army marches to engage Israel. Keep an eye on those trees, because they matter in this story. The text says that day the forest devoured more people than the sword.

The man says the opposite. He tells Joab that if he had jeopardized his own life, “…you would have abandoned me.” So he doesn't think Joab would have stood by him. He also says they heard the king command them to protect Absalom, and he wouldn't raise his hand against the king's son even for a thousand shekels.

That's right. He says that if he had jeopardized his own life, “…you would have abandoned me.” So no, he doesn't think Joab would have stood by him. He also says he wouldn't raise his hand against the son of the king, because they heard the king's command.
That's not what the text says. After Joab blows the ram's horn, “…the troops broke off their pursuit of Israel because Joab had restrained them.” The troops stop their pursuit instead.

All the Israelites fled, each to his home. The people who followed Absalom scatter and head back where they came from. The text says this happens meanwhile, as Absalom is cast into a large pit in the forest.
Amasa is the man Absalom put over the army (2 Samuel 17:25). The text never says anyone makes him king. It says all the Israelites fled, each to his home.

There's no surrender at the gate in these verses. The text says all the Israelites fled, each to his home. David stood beside the gate when his troops marched out, but these Israelites head home instead.
